questions.text: Which mappings between errors and Rust mechanisms are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Recoverable errors use `Result<T, E>`
Unrecoverable errors use `panic!`
Rust does not rely on an exception mechanism in this chapter
Every recoverable error must terminate the program immediately

questions.explanation: Rust distinguishes recoverable and unrecoverable situations: `Result` allows an error to be handled, while `panic!` terminates execution.

questions.text: In which ways can a `panic!` occur? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: By explicitly calling the `panic!` macro
By performing an operation that itself panics
For example, by using an invalid index
Only through `Result::Err`

questions.explanation: A panic can be triggered explicitly or arise in library/language code because of an invalid operation.

questions.text: What does a program do by default on `panic!`?

answers.text: Prints a message, unwinds the stack, cleans up data, and terminates
Ignores the error and continues
Automatically converts the panic into a Result
Restarts the function

questions.explanation: The default behavior includes an error message, stack unwinding, cleanup, and process termination.

questions.text: What does stack unwinding during a panic mean? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Rust walks back through the call stack
Data belonging to encountered functions is cleaned up
It can add extra work
It is the same as an immediate abort without cleanup

questions.explanation: Unwinding walks the stack and performs cleanup, unlike an immediate abort.

questions.text: What does `panic = "abort"` change in a Cargo profile?

answers.text: On panic, the program terminates without unwinding and cleaning up the stack
panic becomes a warning
Result is automatically replaced by Option
Cargo forbids the use of panic!

questions.explanation: Abort mode stops the program immediately; the operating system is left to reclaim the process memory.

questions.text: What is the `RUST_BACKTRACE` environment variable used for?

answers.text: To print the backtrace of calls that led to a panic
To suppress panic
To enable release optimizations
To convert an error into Result

questions.explanation: A backtrace helps reveal the call chain and find the location in your code that led to the panic.

questions.text: Which conditions are mentioned for a useful backtrace? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Backtrace output must be enabled with RUST_BACKTRACE
Detailed information requires debug symbols
Debug symbols are included by default for cargo build/run without --release
The backtrace is guaranteed to be identical on every OS and Rust version

questions.explanation: The material warns that output can vary and notes the role of debug symbols.

questions.text: Where should you start when looking for the cause of a panic in a backtrace?

answers.text: At the first trace line that points to a file in your project
At the very last standard-library line regardless of context
At Cargo.toml
At the declaration of Vec<T>

questions.explanation: The example recommends finding the first line mentioning your own source file and investigating the operation that caused the problem.

questions.text: What happens when accessing `v[99]` if the vector has only three elements? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: It panics because the index is out of bounds
Using `[]` assumes the element exists
A backtrace can show the path to the call site
The operation returns None without a panic

questions.explanation: Indexing with `[]` requires a valid index; `None` is returned by `get`, not by the indexing operator.

questions.text: What roles do type parameters `T` and `E` have in `Result<T, E>`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: T is the type of the success value inside Ok
E is the type of the error value inside Err
They make Result usable with many kinds of success values and errors
T and E must always be the same type

questions.explanation: The generic parameters allow Result to represent many different operations.

questions.text: What can be done when handling `File::open` with `match`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Extract the File from Ok
Take a specific action for a particular Err such as NotFound
Choose another handling path for other errors
`match` automatically guarantees that the file exists

questions.explanation: `match` lets code branch on `Ok` and different kinds of `Err` rather than reducing every failure to one response.

questions.text: Which advantages does an explicit `match` provide when handling `Result`? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Different error kinds can be distinguished
Different actions can be chosen for different Err values
The successful value can be extracted from Ok
`match` is always shorter than unwrap

questions.explanation: A full `match` gives flexible control, although it can be more verbose than helper methods.

questions.text: Which statements about `unwrap()` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: For Ok, it returns the inner value
For Err, it panics
It is a shorter alternative to some match expressions
For Err, it always returns a default value

questions.explanation: The material describes `unwrap` as concise access to a Result with a standard panic response to Err.

questions.text: What useful difference does `expect("...")` have compared with `unwrap()`?

answers.text: It lets you provide a custom panic message for Err
It never panics
It works only with Ok and cannot receive Err
It converts Result into Option

questions.explanation: `expect` has the same basic behavior but adds a meaningful message explaining why success was expected.

questions.text: What does “propagating an error” mean?

answers.text: A function returns the error to its caller instead of fully handling it locally
A function ignores Err and continues
A function always panics
The error is only logged and then lost

questions.explanation: Propagation delegates the decision to the caller, which may have more context for choosing a response.

questions.text: What does `?` do on `Err` for Result? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Returns the error early from the current function
Passes the error to the calling code
Can convert the error type through `From`
Continues to the next line as if no error occurred

questions.explanation: An Err followed by `?` causes an early return; if necessary, `From` converts the error into the type declared by the function's returned Result.

questions.text: How does `?` differ from a manually written `match` when propagating an error?

answers.text: Besides being shorter, an error propagated by `?` goes through `From` conversion
`?` cannot be used with Result
`match` always panics while `?` never does
`?` automatically logs the error

questions.explanation: The material specifically notes the error conversion through `From` when `?` is used.

questions.text: Which approaches can shorten file-reading code while propagating errors? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Using `?` instead of match for each Result
Chaining calls with multiple `?` operators
Using `fs::read_to_string` as an even shorter version
Manually reading every byte is required

questions.explanation: The chapter progressively shortens the code: manual match, `?`, a chain of `?`, and then a ready-made standard-library function.

questions.text: Why can't `?` after `File::open` be used in `fn main() { ... }` that returns `()`?

answers.text: Because the function's return type is incompatible with an early return of a Result error
Because main cannot access files
Because `?` works only inside libraries
Because File::open returns Option

questions.explanation: The `?` operator requires a compatible return type so it can return an error early.

questions.text: Which approaches can fix a function that uses `?` with Result but has an incompatible return type? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Change the return type to a compatible Result when appropriate
Handle the Result with match
Use a suitable Result method instead of `?`
Simply delete the error type from File::open without handling it

questions.explanation: The material suggests changing the signature or handling the Result explicitly/with a method.

questions.text: Which statements about `?` with Option are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: For Some, the inner value becomes the expression result
For None, the function returns None early
Using `?` on Option requires a compatible Option return type
`?` itself converts Option into Result

questions.explanation: Option and Result share a similar `?` pattern but are not automatically converted into one another.

questions.text: What should be done when `Result` and `Option` need to be explicitly converted into one another?

answers.text: Use appropriate methods such as `ok` or `ok_or`
Rely on automatic conversion by `?`
Use only panic!
Add `mut` to the variable

questions.explanation: The material explicitly notes that `?` does not mix Result and Option; conversion is performed explicitly.

questions.text: Which `main` signature permits using `?` on the result of `File::open`?

answers.text: `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>`
`fn main() -> ()` only
`fn main() -> i32` without Result
`fn main() -> String` is required

questions.explanation: The chapter shows a main function returning `Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` and ending with `Ok(())`.

questions.text: Which statements about `Box<dyn Error>` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: For the chapter's purposes, it can be read as 'any kind of error'
It lets the main signature be compatible with different errors
It is used with `Result<(), ...>`
It means the program cannot have errors

questions.explanation: The material simplifies `Box<dyn Error>` as a way to allow different error kinds in `Err`.

questions.text: Why is returning `Result` described as a good default choice for a function that can fail?

answers.text: It leaves the caller to decide how to respond to the error
It guarantees that the function never fails
It prevents the caller from using panic!
It automatically retries the operation

questions.explanation: Result delegates the decision to the caller instead of declaring the situation unrecoverable inside the function.

questions.text: Which consequences of choosing `panic!` instead of Result are noted? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: The code cannot recover execution after the panic
The function itself decides that the situation is unrecoverable
The caller does not receive an ordinary Result from which to choose a strategy
panic gives the caller more control than Result

questions.explanation: Panic removes the caller's ordinary opportunity to recover, while Result preserves it.

questions.text: In which situations can `panic!` or `unwrap` be more appropriate than detailed `Result` handling?

answers.text: Examples, prototypes, and tests
Every library API without exception
Only network requests
Only release builds

questions.explanation: For teaching examples, prototypes, and tests, detailed error handling can obscure the main purpose, so a panic-based approach can be justified.

questions.text: Why can `unwrap` or `expect` be acceptable in tests and prototypes? Select all correct answers.

The code is shorter when demonstrating the main idea
In those contexts, terminating on an unexpected error can be desirable
Because unwrap cannot panic in tests

answers.text: If continuing could be unsafe or meaningless, panic can be justified
A public contract should document conditions whose violation causes panic
When possible, valid states should be encoded in types
Every invalid value should always be silently corrected

questions.text: Why make the inner field of a type representing a validated value private?

answers.text: So external code cannot bypass the invariant by writing an unchecked value directly
So methods of the type itself cannot read the field after construction
So primitive values occupy less memory
So instances of the type automatically implement `Copy`

questions.explanation: A private field forces external code through a controlled construction and mutation API that can preserve the type invariant.

source.locator: Chapter 9 — Creating Custom Types for Validation, pp. 231–234

questions.text: What should a constructor provide for a type that encapsulates a validated range of values? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Validate the input before producing a valid instance
Prevent normally constructed instances from violating the invariant
Let the rest of the program rely on the type invariant
Leave an external path for directly writing an unchecked value into the private field

questions.explanation: The purpose of such a type is to centralize validation at construction and then use the type itself as an invariant guarantee.

source.locator: Chapter 9 — Creating Custom Types for Validation, pp. 231–234

questions.text: What advantage does a specialized parameter type with a guaranteed invariant have over a plain `i32`?

answers.text: The function can rely on the type guarantee instead of repeating the same range validation
The function automatically becomes generic
The compiler forbids reading the inner value even through the type's methods
Every function taking such a parameter automatically returns `Result`

questions.explanation: If a valid instance can only be constructed after validation, functions accepting that type receive the guarantee through the type itself.

questions.text: Which ideas does the custom validation type demonstrate? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: Hide the inner value in a private field
Check constraints during construction
Express valid states through types
Duplicate the same validation in every function that accepts the value

questions.text: What role does `Result` play in handling recoverable errors?

answers.text: It uses the type system to explicitly communicate possible failure and give code a chance to recover
It hides possible failure from the caller
It always means an unrecoverable error
It replaces the type system for fallible functions

questions.explanation: The summary emphasizes that Result makes possible success/failure part of the type and lets calling code respond.

questions.text: Which statements about using `panic!` and `Result` are correct? Select all correct answers.

answers.text: `panic!` signals a state the program cannot handle
Result tells the caller about potential success or failure
Choosing between them appropriately helps produce more reliable code
`panic!` and Result are always interchangeable without changing API meaning

questions.explanation: The chapter summary contrasts unhandleable states with recoverable errors and connects a deliberate choice to program reliability.
